hints: Look carefully at citral and count what can be reduced, two C=C double bonds plus one aldehyde CHO group.
Think about what an excess of H2 with Ni does first, it saturates both C=C bonds to give a saturated aldehyde intermediate V.
Now consider hot, concentrated acidified manganate(VII) under reflux on that saturated aldehyde, and decide what the final oxidation product must be.
walkthrough:
**Spot the functional groups in citral**

Citral has three reactive sites. Two alkene C=C bonds and one aldehyde group, $\text{-CHO}$.

Think of the skeleton as: unsaturated chain + aldehyde end.

**First step, complete hydrogenation to V**

An excess of $\text{H}_2 / \text{Ni}$ adds hydrogen across each C=C bond.

$$\text{R-CH=CH-R' + H}_2 \xrightarrow{\text{Ni}} \text{R-CH}_2\text{-CH}_2\text{-R'}$$

With excess, both double bonds are saturated. The aldehyde survives this step, so V is the saturated aldehyde with formula containing $\text{-CH}_2\text{-CHO}$ at the end.

**Second step, strong oxidation to W**

Hot, concentrated acidified $\text{MnO}_4^-$ under reflux is a powerful oxidiser. It oxidises an aldehyde to a carboxylic acid.

$$\text{R-CHO + [O]} \rightarrow \text{R-CO}_2\text{H}$$

Because V is now fully saturated, there is no C=C left to cleave. So the carbon skeleton stays intact and only $\text{-CHO}$ becomes $\text{-CO}_2\text{H}$. That gives the saturated carboxylic acid.

options.A: This is compound V, not W. It correctly shows both C=C bonds hydrogenated but the aldehyde CHO is still unchanged. Hot concentrated manganate(VII) would oxidise this aldehyde further, so the reaction does not stop here.
options.B: This is exactly W. It has the fully saturated carbon skeleton from complete hydrogenation, and the original aldehyde end has been oxidised to a carboxylic acid CO2H. No cleavage occurs because no double bonds remain for the strong oxidiser to break.
options.C: This is a keto-acid cleavage fragment. It would only form if a C=C bond was still present to be oxidatively cleaved by hot manganate(VII). Since excess H2/Ni has already removed all C=C bonds, this type of chain breaking cannot happen.
options.D: This is ethanedioic acid, $(\text{CO}_2\text{H})_2$. This is the trap for thinking of complete oxidative cleavage of multiple double bonds. It ignores the first hydrogenation step which saturates the molecule and protects the chain from cleavage.
